CHAPTER XVIII

Ghysbrecht Van Swieten could not sleep all night for anxiety. He was
afraid of thunder and lightning, or he would have made one of the party
that searched Peter's house. As soon as the storm ceased altogether,
he crept downstairs, saddled his mule, and rode to the “Three Kings” at
Sevenbergen. There he found his men sleeping, some on the chairs, some
on the tables, some on the floor. He roused them furiously, and heard
the story of their unsuccessful search, interlarded with praises of
their zeal.

“Fool! to let you go without me,” cried the burgomaster. “My life on't
he was there all the time. Looked ye under the girl's bed?”

“No; there was no room for a man there.”

“How know ye that, if ye looked not?” snarled Ghysbrecht. “Ye should
have looked under her bed, and in it too, and sounded all the panels
with your knives. Come, now, get up, and I shall show ye how to search.”

Dierich Brower got up and shook himself. “If you find him, call me a
horse and no man.”

In a few minutes Peter's house was again surrounded.

The fiery old man left his mule in the hands of Jorian Ketel, and, with
Dierich Brower and the others, entered the house.

The house was empty.

Not a creature to be seen, not even Peter. They went upstairs, and
then suddenly one of the men gave a shout, and pointed through Peter's
window, which was open. The others looked, and there, at some little
distance, walking quietly across the fields with Margaret and Martin,
was the man they sought. Ghysbrecht, with an exulting yell, descended
the stairs and flung himself on his mule; and he and his men set off in
hot pursuit.

Ghysbrecht Van Swieten tossed restlessly through the night, his mind churning with unease. Fear of the storm’s wrath kept him from joining the search of Peter’s house, but as soon as the last thunderclap faded, he rose, saddled his mule, and rode hard for Sevenbergen.

At the *Three Kings*, he found his men sprawled in drunken slumber—some slumped over tables, others curled on the floor. With a snarl, he roused them, listening impatiently as they recounted their failure.

*"Fools!"* he spat. *"You let him slip through your fingers. Did you even think to look beneath the girl’s bed?"*

One of the men grunted. *"No space for a man there."*

*"And how would you know if you didn’t look?"* Ghysbrecht’s voice was a whip-crack. *"You should have torn the place apart—searched every corner, tested every panel!"*

Dierich Brower staggered to his feet, rubbing his eyes. *"If you find him now, call me a horse and not a man."*

Within moments, Peter’s house was surrounded once more. Ghysbrecht, his face a mask of grim determination, left his mule with Jorian Ketel and led the charge inside. The rooms stood empty—no Peter, no daughter, no sign of their fugitive guest.

Then a shout rang out. One of the men pointed through the open window, where across the fields, walking calmly beside Margaret and Martin, was the very man they sought.

A triumphant cry burst from Ghysbrecht’s lips. He hurtled down the stairs, vaulted onto his mule, and spurred his men into furious pursuit.
